findings.title: Client error handling bypasses ApiError contract
findings.rationale: The new useDismissAllSuggestions hook calls fetch directly and, on a non-2xx response, throws a plain Error instead of an ApiError. Pages decide what to show from error instanceof ApiError (client/src/app/repos/[repoId]/pulls/page.tsx:111), so a failed bulk-dismiss shows a generic message and loses the server's error code, message, and details. This violates the house rule that client requests surface errors as ApiError.

findings.title: Client mutation throws plain Error on non-2xx, losing server error details
findings.rationale: The new useDismissAllSuggestions hook calls fetch directly and, on a non-2xx response, throws a plain Error. Per house rule 3, all engine requests must throw ApiError (with code/message/details from the server's error body) so pages can show the server's message and status. A plain Error surfaces a generic message and loses the error code, breaking the error-handling contract for this call. The caller (FindingsPanel) will not be able to distinguish a 404 (PR not found) from a 500 (server error) or show the server's reason.

findings.title: Client calls the new route with fetch directly and throws a plain Error on non-2xx, losing the ApiError contract
findings.rationale: Rule 3 of the attached house rules requires that any client code under client/src/ that calls the engine with fetch directly must, on a non-2xx response, throw ApiError (built from the server's { error: { code, message, details } } body) or return the error body as data. The new useDismissAllSuggestions hook does `const res = await fetch(...)` and then `return res.json()` without checking `res.ok` and without constructing an ApiError. On a 4xx/5xx response, `res.json()` will attempt to parse the error body and either throw a generic SyntaxError (if the body is not JSON) or return the parsed error object as if it were success data. Either way, the caller (the FindingsPanel button's onError path) receives a plain Error or a falsy value instead of an ApiError, so the UI shows a generic message and loses the status and error code. This is a real defect that breaks the established error-handling contract for every caller of this hook.

findings.title: Shared contract copies drift: server route added without a matching client-side contract type
findings.rationale: Rule 2 of the attached house rules requires that a change to a shared contract under server/src/vendor/shared/ appear in the matching file under client/src/vendor/shared/ in the same diff. The diff adds a new route `POST /pulls/:id/findings/dismiss-suggestions` to the server's route table (server/src/modules/reviews/routes.ts) but does not touch any file under client/src/vendor/shared/. While the route itself is not a type in vendor/shared, the PR description states the intent is to expose a new endpoint to the client, and the client hook hardcodes the URL string. The two copies of the shared contract now disagree: the server advertises the new route, the client's shared copy does not. This is a silent drift that will compile and look complete on its own, and any future consumer relying on the shared types will not see the new endpoint.

findings.title: Consider documenting the new `tags` field in the PR description
findings.rationale: The PR description says 'Nothing existing changes shape' and 'every finding already in the DB and every agent that doesn't set it keeps working exactly as before.' This is true because `tags` is `nullish()`. However, the description could be more explicit that the field is optional and that existing clients that don't send it will still work. This is a documentation nit, not a contract issue.

findings.title: Tag rendering uses inline styles instead of the existing style object
findings.rationale: The new tag chips use inline styles (`style={{ display: "flex", gap: 4 }}` and `style={{ fontSize: 11, opacity: 0.7 }}`) while the surrounding code uses the `s` style object (e.g. `s.titleRow`, `s.acceptedTag`). For consistency with the rest of the component, consider moving these styles into the `s` object. This is purely cosmetic and costs no caller anything today.

findings.title: Potential duplicate-key collision in tag rendering
findings.rationale: The `key` for each tag span is the tag string itself. If a finding has duplicate tags (e.g. `["flaky", "flaky"]`), React will warn about duplicate keys and may misbehave during reconciliation. Using an index-based key (e.g. `key={`${tag}-${i}`}`) would avoid this. This is a minor hygiene issue and does not affect the contract or break any caller.

matched_title: Unbounded tag strings allow oversized payloads and stored-XSS-adjacent rendering

findings.title: Unbounded tag strings allow oversized payloads and stored-XSS-adjacent rendering
findings.rationale: The new `tags` field is constrained to at most 5 array elements, but each string is unbounded in length. A malicious or buggy agent can attach a single tag of arbitrary size (e.g. megabytes of text), which the client then renders inside a `<span>` via React text interpolation. While React escapes text nodes (so this is not a direct XSS), the unbounded length is a denial-of-service vector: the server stores and returns the finding, and the client renders the full tag string into the DOM, potentially freezing the findings panel or bloating the page. Additionally, the tag is rendered with `#{tag}` and no length truncation, so a very long tag visually breaks the card layout. The contract should cap the per-string length (e.g. `z.string().max(32)`) to match the 'short strings' intent stated in the PR description. This is a WARNING, not CRITICAL, because no existing caller breaks and the rendering is escaped; but it narrows what the client can safely rely on (a bounded tag) and leaves the door open to payload bloat.
